Intervals of a Prediction

Source: R/predict_objects.R
predict_intervals.Rd

The interval argument of predict.StatmodFit() takes an interval object that selects the uncertainty that the interval describes. There are three, and they differ in what the interval is about.

confidence_interval()

the default, with se = TRUE: the interval of a parameter, a predictor or a moment, which carries only the uncertainty of the estimates. It costs one evaluation of the delta method.

group_interval()

the interval of the parameter of a new group, with random = "zero" or "marginal". It adds the variation of the effects of a new group to the uncertainty of the estimates. It costs the delta method plus a quantile of the distribution of the predictor, by closed form under Gaussian priors and by quadrature or Monte Carlo otherwise.

prediction_interval()

the interval of a new observation of the response, with what = "response". It adds the variation of the family itself. The way that the estimation uncertainty enters is set by its argument predictive, described in predictive_distributions. The cost is that of the predictive distribution chosen.

Value

Not applicable: this topic describes the constructors. Each returns an S7 object that inherits from interval_type().

Confidence interval

With the default, an effect set aside by random gives the interval of the typical group's value, and the value of a new group falls outside that interval far more often than the level implies. The interval is built on the scale of the equation and mapped back through the link.

Group interval

A new group's parameter is \(\theta^* = h^{-1}(\eta^*)\), with \(\eta^*\) the typical group's predictor plus its estimation error plus \(z^\top b\), the effects of a new group drawn from the prior, in the parameter's own equation, so a random effect on sigma widens the interval for sigma. Under Gaussian priors the variance of \(\eta^*\) is \(se^2 + z^\top \Sigma_b z\), the standard error that glmmTMB reports at a new level on the link scale. The ends of the interval are quantiles of \(\eta^*\) carried through the inverse link, which is monotone, so they are the quantiles of \(\theta^*\) under any link; under a prior that is not Gaussian they are the quantiles of the mixture of predictive_mixture(). Where the interval of \(\eta^*\) leaves the domain of the link (a square root link and a negative predictor), the ends are NA at that row, with a warning. The standard error is the standard deviation of \(\theta^*\), not the delta method, and is NA where it is not known to exist. The fit is the typical group's value under random = "zero" and the population average under "marginal". The interval implies se = TRUE.

Prediction interval

The family is averaged over the predictors of every parameter, which are taken to be jointly Gaussian (correlated across equations where a label ties them). The ends of the interval are quantiles of that average, and the fit is its median, which every family has, so the family does not need a location parameter. se is the standard deviation of the average, and is NA where the family's variance does not exist. For a discrete family the ends are values of the support, so the coverage is at least the level rather than equal to it. Effects read "conditional" enter with their own estimates, so this is also the interval of a new observation of a group that is present in the fitting data.

Restrictions

group_interval() and prediction_interval() are rejected for a multivariate family and for a model with a structural term. The structural term also rejects random = "zero" and random = "marginal": its level is a recursion read at the predictor, so setting a random effect aside would move the recursion as well.

Under a prior that is not Gaussian, both group_interval() and prediction_interval() read the quantiles of the prior: a Student t prior as a scale mixture of Gaussians; a single univariate prior of another family, where it is the only prior that is not Gaussian, on quantile nodes, which do not depend on the seed; and any other combination of priors by Monte Carlo, which does (see predictive_mixture()). A term that shares a label with an effect read with its own estimate, or with one written inside a subformula, is rejected.

The level of every interval is the argument level of predict.StatmodFit().

See also

confidence_interval(), group_interval(), prediction_interval(), predictive_distributions, predict.StatmodFit().

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(40))
dd$y <- 1 + dd$x + rnorm(40, sd = 0.4)
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
nd <- data.frame(x = c(0.2, 0.8))
predict(fit, what = "mu", newdata = nd, se = TRUE,
        interval = confidence_interval())
#>        fit         se    lower    upper
#> 1 1.283706 0.07987999 1.127144 1.440268
#> 2 1.774511 0.07581109 1.625924 1.923098
predict(fit, what = "response", newdata = nd,
        interval = prediction_interval())
#>        fit        se     lower    upper
#> 1 1.283706 0.3475094 0.5993255 1.968086
#> 2 1.774511 0.3465967 1.0918912 2.457131
